articles.title: How one Haitian entrepreneur found success by supporting all things local
articles.summary: Rébetha Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur; everything grew out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by buying their crops, and encouraging consumers to eat local products.
articles.content:
For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives. Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur. Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.

REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products. Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.

In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things. First, her company adds value. Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders. We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients. Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.

Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur. Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment. “In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work. Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us. Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”

That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause. Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.

It wasn’t easy for Charles, especially at the beginning. In an interview with Chef Cassy, she said she started the business doing papita — breadfruit and banana chips — but spent more than five months making it, every single day, without getting it right. It was only by the sixth month that the papita started coming out well, and she began selling it in supermarkets. After that, things started moving quickly; every day, customers would place more orders — not bad for a small business that began with about USD 8.50, selling papita.

The business has now evolved to the point where it offers a broad range of widely available products: “We sell [our products] in the Grand’Anse department, we sell them in the south, in the west, in several other departments in the country, and we also sell internationally in the United States and Canada.”

Everything has grown out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by purchasing their crops, and encouraging Haitian consumers to eat local products:

Mwen panse li lè li tan pou peyizan yo kapab vann sa yap pwodui. Donk, mwen santi m toujou gen yon responsabilite depi m pase yon kote ki gen dennre, bagay nou yo kap fèt nan andeyò yo, mwen anvi fè yon bagay. Ann manje sa nou pwodui, ann manje sa nou fè. Sa ap pèmèt peyizan yo pa bezwen deplase kite lakay yo pou yo ale lòt kote; yo ka rete nan zòn yo, yap travay, n ap achte, n ap kondisyonnen, nap transfòme, ou menm wap konsome. Konsa, nou tout ap soti gayan, e nap gen yon lòt peyi, nap gen yon lòt kominite.

I think it is time for farmers to be able to sell what they produce. So, I always feel a responsibility whenever I pass by a place that has crops, or things made in the countryside; I want to do something. Let us eat what we produce, let us eat what we make. This will allow farmers to not need to leave their home to go somewhere else; they can stay in their area — they work, we buy, we process, we transform, and you consume. That way, we all win, and we will have another country; another community.

Inside REB Lokal’s processing facility feels different from what one would expect. There are production rooms, transformation rooms, and packaging rooms where employees work in white coats, hairnets, and gloves.

There is also a shop front full of shelves with finished products — now much more diverse than just papita — displayed for sale. There are roasted peanuts, sakalapina (cornmeal with avocados), papita in both chicken and fish flavour, konparet (spiced ginger-coconut cake), corn chanchanm (traditional Haitian sweet, made from roasted corn and peanuts), honey, sugar cane syrup, chocolate powder and balls, cocoa butter, breadfruit, corn, cassava and plantain flour, baby food (made without chemicals under the supervision of paediatricians and nutritionists), alcoholic drinks, fruit juice, and castor oil.

To Rébetha Charles, who grew up in an idyllic rural community, the work of REB Lokal is close to her heart. Yet, running a business in an insecure country comes with its challenges. Gangs’ control of the main roads can make delivery slow and limit production, as the lack of access prevents products from reaching many communities. A true entrepreneur, Charles finds ways around such obstacles as best she can. She still believes that Haiti has a future, so she perseveres, believing the impossible can become possible through vision and sheer willpower.
articles.reasoning: This article highlights a Haitian entrepreneur who supports local farmers by creating a sustainable agri-food business that adds value to local produce, improves farmers' livelihoods, and encourages consumption of local products. The story has broad social and economic significance for Haiti's community and rural development, with detailed context about the challenges and impact of the enterprise.
articles.personality_title: Haitian entrepreneur boosts local farming with homegrown food business
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Haiti has long depended on imported goods, making it hard for local farmers to compete. This situation began in the 1990s after agreements with international lenders lowered tariffs on foreign products. Along with other problems like political instability and violence, this has weakened Haiti’s farming and food production.

**What happened** – Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old agronomy graduate from Jérémie, started a company called REB Lokal. She buys crops from nearly 2,000 small Haitian farmers and turns them into healthy, local food products. She launched the business in 2020 after leaving a difficult work environment. Starting with breadfruit and banana chips, her products now include many Haitian traditional foods and are sold across Haiti and even in the US and Canada.

**Impact** – REB Lokal helps farmers sell their crops without losing them to spoilage, adding value by processing fresh, natural foods that follow local traditions. The company avoids chemicals and supports over 20 employees. This work encourages Haitians to eat local food and helps farmers stay in their communities instead of moving away for work.

**What's next step** – Rébetha plans to keep growing the business despite challenges like gang violence and poor roads that slow deliveries. She hopes her example will inspire others and help build a stronger, more self-sufficient food system in Haiti.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By turning local crops into quality foods, Rébetha Charles is creating new opportunities for Haitian farmers and promoting the country’s rich food traditions.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une entrepreneure haïtienne soutient les agriculteurs locaux avec une entreprise alimentaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Haïti dépend depuis longtemps des produits importés, ce qui rend la concurrence difficile pour les agriculteurs locaux. Cette situation a commencé dans les années 1990 après des accords avec des institutions financières internationales qui ont abaissé les tarifs sur les produits étrangers. Avec d’autres problèmes comme l’instabilité politique et la violence, cela a affaibli l’agriculture et la production alimentaire en Haïti.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Rébetha Charles, diplômée en agronomie de 38 ans originaire de Jérémie, a lancé une entreprise appelée REB Lokal. Elle a commencé son activité en 2020 après avoir quitté un environnement de travail difficile. Partant de chips de fruit à pain et de banane, ses produits incluent maintenant de nombreuses spécialités haïtiennes et sont vendus en Haïti, ainsi qu’aux États-Unis et au Canada.

**Impact** – REB Lokal aide les agriculteurs à vendre leurs récoltes sans pertes, en ajoutant de la valeur grâce à la transformation d’aliments frais et naturels selon les traditions locales. L’entreprise évite les produits chimiques et emploie plus de 20 personnes. Ce travail encourage les Haïtiens à consommer local et aide les agriculteurs à rester dans leurs communautés au lieu de partir chercher du travail.

**Prochaine étape** – Rébetha prévoit de continuer à développer son entreprise malgré les défis comme la violence des gangs et les routes difficiles qui ralentissent les livraisons. Elle espère que son exemple inspirera d’autres personnes et contribuera à construire un système alimentaire plus fort et autonome en Haïti.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – En transformant les récoltes locales en aliments de qualité, Rébetha Charles crée de nouvelles opportunités pour les agriculteurs haïtiens et valorise les traditions culinaires du pays.
articles.personality_title_es: Una emprendedora haitiana impulsa la agricultura local con su negocio de alimentos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Haití ha dependido durante mucho tiempo de productos importados, lo que dificulta la competencia para los agricultores locales. Esta situación comenzó en los años 90 tras acuerdos con instituciones financieras internacionales que redujeron los aranceles sobre productos extranjeros. Junto con otros problemas como la inestabilidad política y la violencia, esto ha debilitado la agricultura y la producción de alimentos en Haití.

**Qué pasó** – Rébetha Charles, una ingeniera agrónoma de 38 años originaria de Jérémie, fundó una empresa llamada REB Lokal. Ella compra cultivos de casi 2,000 pequeños agricultores haitianos y los convierte en productos alimenticios locales saludables. Empezó el negocio en 2020 después de dejar un trabajo difícil. Comenzó con chips de fruto de pan y plátano, y ahora sus productos incluyen muchas comidas tradicionales haitianas que se venden en Haití, Estados Unidos y Canadá.

**Impacto** – REB Lokal ayuda a los agricultores a vender sus cultivos sin pérdidas, agregando valor al procesar alimentos frescos y naturales siguiendo tradiciones locales. La empresa evita químicos y emplea a más de 20 personas. Su trabajo anima a los haitianos a consumir productos locales y ayuda a los agricultores a quedarse en sus comunidades en lugar de irse a buscar trabajo.

**Próximo paso** – Rébetha planea seguir creciendo a pesar de los desafíos como la violencia de pandillas y las malas carreteras que dificultan las entregas. Espera que su ejemplo inspire a otros y ayude a construir un sistema alimentario más fuerte y autosuficiente en Haití.

**Resumen en una frase** – Al transformar cultivos locales en alimentos de calidad, Rébetha Charles crea nuevas oportunidades para los agricultores haitianos y promueve las tradiciones culinarias del país.

articles.title: The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Not every vegetable belongs in a backyard garden. Some take up space, demand attention, and still cost more to grow than to buy once you factor in seeds, soil, and the time it takes. But some crops genuinely save you money, and if your grocery bill has been creeping […]
The post The 7 best vegetables to plant if you want to offset rising grocery costs first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Not every vegetable belongs in a backyard garden. Some take up space, demand attention, and still cost more to grow than to buy once you factor in seeds, soil, and the time it takes. But some crops genuinely save you money, and if your grocery bill has been creeping up, those are the ones to plant.

Robert Westerfield, a horticulture specialist at the University of Georgia, and Damon Abdi, assistant professor at the Louisiana State University AgCenter, both weigh in on what pays off at home. Seven vegetables made the list.

Herbs

Westerfield describes herbs as “so forgiving,” and the economics back that up. Fresh herbs are among the most expensive produce per ounce at the grocery store, and a purchased bunch often goes partly to waste before you get through it. A plant in your garden means you take what you need, when you need it, and nothing wilts in the back of the drawer.

Rosemary is an especially smart first choice. It’s evergreen, drought-tolerant, and flowers in a way that looks good in the garden, not just the kitchen. Abdi recommends it specifically because you can harvest on demand rather than buying packaged herbs that “can languish if left unused.”

Peppers

Peppers are resilient in a way that a lot of vegetables aren’t. Westerfield calls them cold-hardy and says they “come through disease and insects better than anything.” They need consistent water and well-draining soil, but they produce over a long season, and fresh peppers aren’t cheap.

Tomatoes

Cherry tomatoes are the easiest entry point. Westerfield recommends starting with one or two plants, which he says will supply you through the season with “less trouble than the larger ones.” Give them a trellis or something to climb and they’ll mostly look after themselves.

Green beans

Green beans can be seeded directly into the ground, no transplants needed, and they produce heavily once they get going. “If you take care of them, you can harvest into the summer,” Westerfield says. They’re a forgiving crop and a reliable one, which makes them a sensible place to start.

Asparagus

Asparagus is a different kind of investment. Both Westerfield and Abdi recommend it, but the payoff takes patience. The first year or two are about establishment. By the third and fourth year, the harvest grows. A well-maintained bed can produce for up to 20 years.

“Asparagus is pricey up front and takes a little time and effort, but it’s perennial once you get it established,” Westerfield says. “You’ll have it basically for life. They can keep on loving you as long as you love them.” Abdi notes that asparagus does best where winters are cool, and that gardeners in warmer climates should look for cold-hardy varieties bred for those conditions.

Cucumbers

Cucumbers produce heavily and pickle well, so a good summer harvest can stretch well into winter with a few jars on the shelf. Keep them off the ground by growing vertically, and they’ll stay healthier through the season.

Squash

Squash is easy to grow, though squash bugs and squash vine borers can derail a season quickly if you let them get ahead of you. Stay on top of those two pests, and you’ll come away with a solid harvest.

One honest caveat

Westerfield is all in on home growing, but he’s clear-eyed about the work involved. It takes time, effort, and real upfront cost. “You know what you put on it and you know where it comes from,” he says. “Usually, the taste and quality are outstanding. There’s nothing quite like fresh tomatoes and sweet corn out of the garden.” The garden only saves money if you’re harvesting and eating what you planted, so starting with the vegetables your household already goes through most is how you make sure it does.

articles.personality_title: 7 vegetables that can help you save money on groceries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Grocery prices have been rising, making it harder for many families to afford fresh produce. Growing your own vegetables can be a way to save money, but not all plants are worth the effort or cost.

**What happened** – Experts from the University of Georgia and Louisiana State University shared their advice on the seven best vegetables to grow at home for saving money. These include herbs like rosemary, peppers, cherry tomatoes, green beans, asparagus, cucumbers, and squash. Each vegetable has qualities that make it easier to grow, productive, and cost-effective.

**Impact** – Growing these vegetables at home can reduce grocery bills because they are often expensive to buy fresh. For example, herbs like rosemary last longer and can be picked as needed, avoiding waste. Asparagus takes time to grow but can produce for up to 20 years, providing long-term savings. Vegetables like peppers and green beans are hardy and produce a lot, making them reliable choices.

**What's next step** – People who want to save money by gardening should start with vegetables their families already enjoy. They should be prepared for some upfront work and cost but can expect fresh, tasty produce. Over time, these gardens can grow to provide a steady supply of food, helping households manage food expenses.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Growing certain easy and productive vegetables at home can help families lower grocery costs while enjoying fresh, high-quality food.
articles.personality_title_fr: 7 légumes à cultiver pour économiser sur les courses
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les prix des produits alimentaires frais augmentent, ce qui complique l’achat pour beaucoup de familles. Cultiver ses propres légumes peut aider à économiser, mais toutes les plantes ne sont pas faciles ou rentables à cultiver.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des experts de l’Université de Géorgie et de l’Université d’État de Louisiane ont conseillé sur les sept meilleurs légumes à cultiver chez soi pour faire des économies. Il s’agit des herbes comme le romarin, des poivrons, des tomates cerises, des haricots verts, des asperges, des concombres et des courges. Ces légumes sont faciles à cultiver, productifs et économiques.

**Impact** – Cultiver ces légumes à la maison peut diminuer la facture des courses car ils sont souvent chers à l’achat. Par exemple, les herbes comme le romarin durent longtemps et on peut les cueillir au besoin, évitant le gaspillage. Les asperges demandent du temps mais peuvent produire jusqu’à 20 ans, offrant une économie durable. Les poivrons et haricots verts sont résistants et produisent beaucoup, ce qui les rend fiables.

**Prochaine étape** – Ceux qui veulent économiser avec un potager doivent commencer par les légumes qu’ils mangent déjà. Il faut prévoir du travail et un coût au départ, mais on peut s’attendre à des légumes frais et savoureux. Avec le temps, le potager peut fournir une nourriture régulière et aider à gérer le budget alimentaire.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Cultiver certains légumes faciles et productifs chez soi peut aider les familles à réduire leurs dépenses alimentaires tout en profitant de produits frais et de qualité.
articles.personality_title_es: 7 verduras para cultivar y ahorrar en la compra
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los precios de los alimentos frescos están subiendo, lo que dificulta que muchas familias puedan comprarlos. Cultivar verduras en casa puede ayudar a ahorrar dinero, pero no todas las plantas son fáciles o rentables de cultivar.

**Qué pasó** – Expertos de la Universidad de Georgia y la Universidad Estatal de Luisiana recomendaron las siete mejores verduras para cultivar en casa y ahorrar dinero. Estas incluyen hierbas como el romero, pimientos, tomates cherry, ejotes, espárragos, pepinos y calabazas. Cada verdura es fácil de cultivar, produce bien y es económica.

**Impacto** – Cultivar estas verduras en casa puede reducir la cuenta del supermercado porque suelen ser caras frescas. Por ejemplo, las hierbas como el romero duran mucho y se pueden cortar cuando se necesiten, evitando desperdicios. Los espárragos tardan en crecer pero pueden producir hasta 20 años, ofreciendo ahorro a largo plazo. Los pimientos y ejotes son resistentes y producen mucho, haciéndolos opciones confiables.

**Próximo paso** – Las personas que quieran ahorrar con un huerto deben comenzar con verduras que ya comen en casa. Deben estar preparados para algo de trabajo y gasto inicial, pero pueden esperar verduras frescas y sabrosas. Con el tiempo, el huerto puede proveer comida constante y ayudar a controlar el gasto en alimentos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Cultivar ciertas verduras fáciles y productivas en casa puede ayudar a las familias a reducir sus gastos en comida mientras disfrutan de alimentos frescos y de calidad.
